cards.text: The prophet Jeremiah is telling this one himself. After Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, carries Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah off to Babylon, along with Judah's officials and Jerusalem's craftsmen and metalsmiths, the LORD shows Jeremiah something. It's sitting right in front of the temple of the LORD.

cards.question: What does the LORD show Jeremiah in front of the temple?

answers.text: A branch from an almond tree

cards.text: One basket has very good figs, like those that ripen early. Those are front-row, Display Case, take-a-picture figs.

cards.question: The figs in the other basket are a little rough, but they're still fine to eat.

cards.text: The LORD asks Jeremiah what he sees, and Jeremiah answers with one word: "Figs!" I have NEVER answered anything that fast, friend, and I'm a stamper. I only know how to do one thing.
Then the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah. Turns out those two baskets are about people.

cards.question: In the LORD's message to Jeremiah, who are like the good figs?
The LORD says He Himself sent the exiles from Judah away to the land of the Chaldeans.

cards.text: Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer, and the only one keeping an eye on me was a dead battery. These exiles get WAY better: God says He'll keep His eyes on them for good and bring them back to this land.

cards.question: God promises the exiles: I will ___ them up and not tear them down; I will ___ them and not uproot them.

cards.text: Then God goes deeper than building and planting. He says He'll give the exiles a heart to know Him, that He is the LORD.

cards.question: God says the exiles will be His people and He will be their God. What reason does He give?

answers.text: They will return to Him with all their heart
They will build Him a new temple in Babylon
They will win their land back in battle

cards.text: Now the other basket. Like the bad figs, so bad they can't be eaten, that's how God says He'll deal with Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the people of Jerusalem still left in the land.

cards.question: Besides Zedekiah, his officials and the ones still in the land, who else from Jerusalem does God put with the bad figs?
Wherever God banishes the people He compares to bad figs, He says He'll make them a ___ to all the kingdoms of the earth.

cards.text: No jokes on this one, friend. God says He'll send sword and famine and plague against them.

cards.question: God says the sword, famine and plague will keep coming until the people He compares to bad figs have perished from the land He gave them and their fathers.

findings.problem: The card says Jeremiah 'answers with one word: "Figs!"' In Jeremiah 24:3 he goes on: 'The good figs are very good, but the bad figs are very bad, so bad they cannot be eaten.' So the text shows the one-word claim is untrue, and the rest of his answer is dropped.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The joke 'I have NEVER answered anything that fast, friend, and I'm a stamper. I only know how to do one thing' doesn't hold together. Being a stamper that does one thing has nothing to do with answering a question quickly, so the comparison doesn't share the action and won't click. It also depends on the untrue 'one word' setup.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action. ... It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining. If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The joke 'the only one keeping an eye on me was a dead battery' adds a new detail to the junk drawer backstory, and that detail goes against it. In the backstory the drawer friends were 'all in it together,' and he welcomed every newcomer. Made-up joke moments are allowed only around his bakery.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: 'God promises the exiles:' presents the words as spoken to the exiles. In Jeremiah 24:4-5 the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah, and the exiles are spoken about, not to. The card should say God promises this about the exiles, or speaks to Jeremiah.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The wrong answers 'blessing' and 'light' are positive, while the sentence describes judgment on the people compared to bad figs. Their tone doesn't match, so 'horror' stands out as the only possible fit.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin's voice is thin across the walkthrough. Cards 6, 11 and 13 are plain narration with no reaction or personality. The only jokes, on cards 3, 5 and 9, are mild or muddled. Several moments could carry a real laugh without muddying a fact, like the very good versus very bad baskets or the exiles being the good ones.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
